title: Meskel in Ethiopia
author: Sisay Tilahun
excerpt: Every year in Ethiopia, September brings one of the country’s most beautiful and deeply meaningful religious celebrations: Meskel, the Finding of the True Cross. It is a time when communities come together for prayer, singing,…

blocks.text: Every year in Ethiopia, September brings one of the country’s most beautiful and deeply meaningful religious celebrations: Meskel, the Finding of the True Cross. It is a time when communities come together for prayer, singing, dancing, feasting, and the lighting of enormous bonfires known as Damera.

Meskel is celebrated on September 17 according to the Ethiopian calendar, which corresponds to September 27 in the Gregorian calendar. The festival takes place at the end of the rainy season, when the countryside begins to turn green and the bright yellow Adey Ababa, or Meskel daisies, cover the landscape. For many Ethiopians, this makes Meskel feel like both a religious celebration and a joyful welcome to a new season.
The Story Behind Meskel

The story of Meskel goes back to the fourth century and is traditionally associated with Empress Helena, the mother of Constantine the Great. According to Christian tradition, Helena travelled to Jerusalem in search of the cross on which Jesus Christ was crucified.

Unable to discover where the cross had been buried, tradition says that Helena prayed for divine guidance. She then ordered a large fire to be prepared and burned incense. As the story is told, the smoke rose into the air and pointed toward the place where the True Cross had been buried.
Following the direction of the smoke, the cross was eventually discovered beneath the ground, together with two other crosses. Tradition identifies one of the three as the True Cross of Christ.

The story of how a portion of the True Cross eventually came to Ethiopia is deeply connected with Ethiopian Orthodox tradition. According to Ethiopian legend, the sacred relic was brought to the country and eventually associated with Gishen Mariam, a monastery in the Wollo region.

Gishen Mariam is traditionally believed to be the resting place of a piece of the True Cross. The monastery is also associated with an ancient volume that records the story of the True Cross and how it came to Ethiopia. For Ethiopian Orthodox Christians, the site remains an important place of pilgrimage and devotion.
The Damera: The Heart of the Celebration
The most recognizable symbol of Meskel is the enormous Damera, the ceremonial bonfire that stands at the center of the celebration.

In the days leading up to Meskel, communities gather wood and prepare the bonfire. At the top is usually a large cross decorated with flowers, particularly the yellow Meskel daisies that bloom throughout Ethiopia around this time of year.

As evening approaches, the atmosphere becomes increasingly festive. Priests dressed in colorful ceremonial robes gather around the Damera, accompanied by singing, chanting, dancing, and prayers. The bonfire is blessed before it is finally set alight.
When the flames rise into the night sky, the celebration becomes a spectacular sight. Families, friends, and communities gather around the fire, sharing food, singing and celebrating together.

For visitors, witnessing a Damera is a wonderful way to experience an important part of Ethiopian religious and cultural life—not simply as a festival to observe, but as a community celebration filled with faith, tradition, music, and togetherness.
The Golden Flowers of Meskel
One of the most beautiful natural symbols associated with Meskel is the Adey Ababa, the bright yellow flower that blooms around the end of the rainy season.

The appearance of these flowers across the Ethiopian countryside adds a special beauty to the festival. Their arrival is traditionally associated with the beginning of a new season and is often seen as a symbol of renewal and hope.

As the rains come to an end, the landscape changes dramatically. Green fields, fresh vegetation, and fields of yellow flowers create a colorful backdrop for Meskel celebrations throughout the country.
This connection between the religious festival and the changing landscape is one of the reasons Meskel feels so uniquely Ethiopian.
Meskel: Faith, History and Community

Although Meskel has a deeply religious foundation, the celebration also brings together many aspects of Ethiopian culture. It is a time for communities to gather, families to share meals, young people to sing and dance, and neighbors to celebrate together.

The sound of traditional songs and prayers, the movement of priests around the Damera, the warmth of the fire, and the sight of thousands of people gathering together create an atmosphere that is difficult to describe in words.

For travelers interested in Ethiopian history, Orthodox Christianity, culture, and traditional celebrations, Meskel offers an opportunity to experience Ethiopia during one of its most important annual festivals.
Experience Meskel in Ethiopia

At Sador Ethiopia Tours, we believe that experiencing Ethiopia is about more than visiting famous historical sites. It is also about connecting with the people, traditions, stories, faith, and celebrations that have shaped the country for generations.
Meskel offers exactly that kind of experience—a celebration where ancient tradition, religious devotion, music, community, and the beauty of the Ethiopian landscape come together.
If you are planning to visit Ethiopia around Meskel, we would be happy to help you experience the celebration while also exploring the country’s history, culture, landscapes, and local communities.
Come and experience Meskel in Ethiopia not simply as a festival, but as a living tradition.

title: From Asosa to Lalibela: A Journey of Love
author: Sisay Tilahun
excerpt: An Ethiopian Biological Family Reunion with Ethiopian Family Search & Sador Ethiopia Tours Some journeys take you to beautiful places. Others bring you closer to the people you have been waiting to meet.

blocks.text: An Ethiopian Biological Family Reunion with Ethiopian Family Search & Sador Ethiopia Tours
Some journeys take you to beautiful places. Others bring you closer to the people you have been waiting to meet.

There are some journeys in life that are difficult to describe with words. They are not simply about visiting a new country, discovering beautiful landscapes, or exploring historical places. They are about people, family, love, and the emotions that stay with you long after the journey ends. This was one of those journeys.

In September 2026, I had the privilege of accompanying an amazing Italian adoptive family on a very special trip to Ethiopia. Their two adopted children, a 23-year-old young woman and her 15-year-old brother, were returning to Ethiopia to meet their biological family. Their journey brought them from Italy to Addis Ababa, then to the rural communities around Asosa in the Benishangul-Gumuz region, and later to some of the most beautiful historical and cultural destinations in northern Ethiopia.
For me, this was much more than a tour. It was a family reunion, a heritage journey, and a beautiful reminder of how powerful family connections can be.
How This Beautiful Journey Began

The story actually started several months before the family arrived in Ethiopia. On January 21, 2025, the Italian adoptive family hired me through Ethiopian Family Search to help search for the biological family of their two adopted children. The search took us to Amba 1, a rural area approximately 13 kilometers from Asosa town in the Benishangul-Gumuz region of western Ethiopia.

After several days of searching, I was able to find their grandparents, uncles, and aunts. Finding the family was a very important moment, but I knew that the real meaning of the search would come later, when the children would finally have the opportunity to meet their Ethiopian relatives.
A few months after the search, the family planned their reunion trip. On September 7, 2026, they arrived in Ethiopia, ready to meet the people they had been waiting for.
A Warm Welcome to Ethiopia

I still remember welcoming the family at Bole International Airport in Addis Ababa. After their long flight from Italy, we took them to their reserved hotel so they could rest. They were tired from the journey, but there was also excitement in the air. They knew that something very special was about to begin. After they had some rest, we decided to visit two important places in Addis Ababa: Holy Trinity Cathedral and the Ethnological Museum at Addis Ababa University.

Holy Trinity Cathedral, also known as Kidist Selassie, is one of the most important Ethiopian Orthodox churches in Addis Ababa. The cathedral is known for its beautiful architecture, religious artwork, and its place in Ethiopia’s modern history. It is also the burial place of Emperor Haile Selassie and Empress Menen Asfaw. Visiting the cathedral gave the family a first glimpse into Ethiopia’s religious traditions and royal history.

From there, we continued to the Ethnological Museum, located in the former palace of Emperor Haile Selassie within Addis Ababa University. This museum is a wonderful place to discover the diversity of Ethiopian culture. Inside, visitors can see traditional household items, musical instruments, religious objects, and exhibitions showing the lifestyles and traditions of different Ethiopian communities. We also had the opportunity to see the former royal bedroom, which gives visitors a glimpse into the country’s imperial past.

After our visits, we were invited to lunch by the children’s older uncle, who lives in Addis Ababa. We spent a beautiful time together with his wife and three children. There was delicious food, conversation, laughter, and the warmth of an Ethiopian family welcoming their relatives home. It was a lovely beginning to the reunion, and it made the family feel even more connected to Ethiopia. After lunch, we returned to the hotel so everyone could get enough rest before our early flight to Asosa the following morning.
The Moment We Had All Been Waiting For: Asosa

The next morning, we flew from Addis Ababa to Asosa. For the children, this was not just another domestic flight. We were traveling toward the place where their biological family was waiting for them. Asosa is the capital of Benishangul-Gumuz Regional State, located in western Ethiopia. The area is known for its green landscapes, rural communities, and the rich cultural heritage of the Berta people. But for this family, Asosa meant something much deeper. It was the place where their story was beginning to reconnect.

After arriving, we checked into our hotel and prepared to drive to the grandparents’ home in the rural area. But before we could leave, the children’s uncles came to welcome us at the hotel. They greeted the family with so much happiness and excitement. It was a beautiful surprise, and the reunion had already begun before we even reached the grandparents’ house. In the afternoon, we drove toward the family home. As we arrived, the grandparents and relatives had prepared a huge and heartfelt welcome. There was so much food, drinks, and the warmth of people who had been waiting a long time for this moment.

I cannot fully describe the emotions of that first meeting. There were tears, laughter, embraces, and moments when everyone simply looked at each other. The children were finally standing in front of their grandparents, uncles, and aunts. The biological family was able to welcome them home, and the adoptive family was able to share in this incredible moment. We ate, drank, played, talked, and enjoyed every moment together. The biological family had prepared an enormous amount of food for us. Their generosity and hospitality were unforgettable. It was the kind of welcome that comes from the heart.

After spending half a day together, we returned to our hotel for the night. Everyone was tired, but it was the kind of tiredness that comes after a day filled with happiness and overwhelming emotions.
A Day Full of Laughter, Family, and the Beauty of Asosa

The following morning, we returned to the grandparents’ home. This time, we had the whole day to spend together, and it became one of the most memorable days of the entire trip. We shared breakfast, coffee, conversation, and many beautiful moments with the family. The children were getting to know their relatives, and everyone was enjoying the time together. There was a natural connection between the siblings and their biological family that was beautiful to witness.

In the afternoon, we took a short excursion to the nearby Hoha River Waterfalls. The surrounding landscape was beautiful, and the visit gave us an opportunity to enjoy the natural scenery of the Asosa area. We took pictures, enjoyed the fresh air, and spent time together away from the family home. Along the way, we also met young Berta girls selling corn by the roadside. It was a simple but special moment that allowed the family to experience a little of everyday life in the area.

My friend Dagi joined us as our Italian-speaking translator. Since I do not speak Italian, he helped us communicate with the family and made the whole journey easier. But Dagi was not only a translator. He quickly became part of the fun. At one point, he challenged the young adoptee to a running competition. Watching them run and laugh together was so much fun. On the way back to the grandparents’ house, I even challenged the young adoptee to a push-up competition. We were all laughing, and those little moments made the day even more special. These are the moments I love about my work. A family reunion is not only about the big emotional meetings. It is also about the small moments of laughter, friendship, and happiness that people remember forever. That evening, one of the children’s uncles invited us to dinner at his home in Asosa town. We enjoyed delicious food, Ethiopian coffee, conversation, and laughter with his family. Once again, we were welcomed with so much love and generosity. Later that evening, we returned to our hotel, carrying another day of beautiful memories.
A Candlelight Prayer for Their Biological Mother

During our time in Asosa, we also experienced one of the most emotional moments of the entire journey. After the first meeting with the family, we learned that the children’s biological mother had passed away. I was the person who had to tell the children this heartbreaking news. It was an incredibly difficult moment for me. I knew how much they had hoped to meet their mother, and I felt the weight of having to share this painful truth with them. The following morning, before visiting the grandparents’ house, we arranged a candlelight prayer at a nearby church in memory of their biological mother. We lit candles, prayed, and remembered her. It was a quiet and deeply emotional moment. Although she was no longer with us, her memory was present throughout the reunion. The children were able to honor their mother and feel connected to her family and heritage. This was one of the moments I will never forget. Some experiences are not about taking pictures or visiting attractions. They are about standing beside people during the most difficult and meaningful moments of their lives.
The Hardest Goodbye in Asosa

Our final day in Asosa arrived much too quickly. In the morning, we returned to the grandparents’ house for one more visit. We shared breakfast and coffee together, enjoying the last precious hours with the family. Everyone knew that saying goodbye would be difficult. After our time with the grandparents, we returned to Asosa town for lunch at one of the children’s aunt’s homes. We met her family, shared a meal, drank coffee, and spent time playing with the children. The atmosphere was full of love and happiness, but we all knew that the time to leave was approaching. When we finally drove to the airport, the emotions became overwhelming. The biological family had welcomed the children with so much love. The siblings had built beautiful memories with their grandparents, uncles, and aunts. Now they had to say goodbye. There were tears, hugs, and long goodbyes. We took family group photographs to preserve the memories of this very special reunion. It was one of the hardest moments of the journey. But it was also a beautiful reminder that love and family connections can cross borders, distance, and many years apart.\ We took our evening flight back to Addis Ababa, arriving around 9:00 PM after a two-hour delay. The family returned to the hotel to get a few hours of rest because we had another early flight the next morning.
Discovering the Beauty of Bahir Dar and Lake Tana

After our emotional days in Asosa, we continued our journey to Bahir Dar, the beautiful lakeside city on the shores of Lake Tana. Our driver was waiting for us at the airport. Since it was still early in the morning and our hotel check-in time had not yet arrived, we decided to use our time wisely and visit one of Ethiopia’s most spectacular natural attractions: Tis Abay, the famous Blue Nile Falls. We drove toward the town of Tis Abay, completed the necessary entrance arrangements, and continued to the waterfall site. From where we stopped our car, we took a gentle walk of approximately 30–40 minutes to reach the falls. The walk itself was beautiful, with amazing landscapes and views of the surrounding countryside. And then we reached the waterfall. The Blue Nile Falls, locally known as Tis Issat, meaning “Smoking Water,” is one of Ethiopia’s most famous natural attractions. The falls are formed where the Abay River plunges over a dramatic cliff, creating a spectacular display of rushing water and mist. The landscape around the falls was breathtaking. The sound of the water, the green scenery, and the impressive gorge made it a memorable destination for everyone. We spent a wonderful time taking pictures, enjoying the scenery, and appreciating the beauty of Ethiopia.

After our visit, we walked back to our car and drove to Bahir Dar. We sent our luggage to the hotel with our driver and went for lunch at Kuriftu Resort. It was a beautiful place to relax after our morning excursion. In the afternoon, we took a boat trip across Lake Tana to visit the monastery of Azwa Mariam on the Zege Peninsula. Lake Tana is the largest lake in Ethiopia and the source of the Abay River, which is known internationally as the Blue Nile. The lake is famous for its beautiful scenery, islands, monasteries, and diverse wildlife. It is also an important part of Ethiopian history and culture. The boat journey itself was a wonderful experience. We enjoyed the peaceful waters, beautiful views, and the surrounding landscape. When we reached the Zege Peninsula, we visited Azwa Mariam, an Ethiopian Orthodox monastery known for its religious heritage and traditional church architecture. The monasteries around Lake Tana are famous for their ancient religious traditions, beautiful paintings, and spiritual importance. Visiting these places gave the family a deeper understanding of Ethiopia’s Orthodox Christian heritage and the role of Lake Tana in the country’s history. During our boat trip, we also had the opportunity to see hippos in Lake Tana. It was a wonderful wildlife experience and another highlight of our day. Seeing these magnificent animals in their natural environment made our visit even more memorable. We also had the chance to see the outlet of Lake Tana, where the Abay River begins its journey. As an Ethiopian, I prefer to call it the Abay River, the name we use at home. The Abay is one of Ethiopia’s most important rivers and plays a major role in the country’s geography, agriculture, and history. Standing by the water and looking at the beautiful landscape was a special moment for all of us. After our boat trip, we returned to Bahir Dar and checked into our hotel, Blue Nile Avanti Hotel, for the night.
Gondar: Walking Through Ethiopia’s Royal History

The next morning, after breakfast, we began our journey to Gondar. At approximately 8:30 AM, we drove around 180 kilometers from Bahir Dar to the historic city. Gondar is one of Ethiopia’s most important historical cities. It was the imperial capital of Ethiopia for more than 250 years, beginning in the 17th century. The city is famous for its castles, churches, royal history, and unique architecture. After arriving, we stopped for lunch at a local restaurant. Then we continued to the Royal Enclosure, one of the most famous historical attractions in Ethiopia. The Royal Enclosure is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and contains a remarkable collection of castles and buildings from the Gondarine period. The most famous structure is the castle of Emperor Fasilides, a magnificent stone building that reflects a combination of Ethiopian, Portuguese, and other architectural influences. The complex also includes palaces, libraries, banquet halls, and other royal buildings. Walking through the Royal Enclosure was an amazing experience for the family. They were fascinated by the history, architecture, and stories of Ethiopia’s former kings and queens. After visiting the Royal Enclosure, we drove to Fasilides’ Bath. This historic site is famous for the annual Ethiopian Orthodox Timkat celebration, which commemorates the baptism of Jesus Christ. During the Timkat festival, the bath is filled with water, and thousands of people gather to celebrate with prayer, music, dancing, and religious ceremonies. The site is one of the most important places in Ethiopia for this celebration. Although we were not visiting during Timkat, it was fascinating to learn about the history and traditions connected to this special place. Our next stop was Debre Birhan Selassie Church, one of the most famous churches in Gondar. The church is renowned for its beautiful Ethiopian Orthodox paintings, especially the famous ceiling decorated with rows of angel faces.

The paintings are an important example of Ethiopian religious art. The church also has a rich history and is an important place of worship for the Ethiopian Orthodox community. The family enjoyed learning about the church, its artwork, and its spiritual significance. After our sightseeing, we returned to our reserved hotel, Gondar Hills Resort. We relaxed, enjoyed the beautiful surroundings, and prepared for the next day’s journey to Lalibela.
Lalibela: A Journey into Ethiopia’s Sacred Heritage

The next morning, we drove to Gondar Airport to take our flight to Lalibela. After arriving at Lalibela Airport, our driver was waiting for us. We drove a few kilometers into town and checked into our hotel. Lalibela is one of Ethiopia’s most famous historical and religious destinations. It is home to the extraordinary rock-hewn churches built during the reign of King Lalibela in the 12th and 13th centuries. These churches were carved directly into the rock, creating an architectural masterpiece unlike anywhere else in the world. Lalibela is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most important pilgrimage destinations for Ethiopian Orthodox Christians.

After lunch and a short rest, we began our visit to the rock-hewn churches at approximately 2:00 PM. We started with the first group of churches, including Bete Medhane Alem, the largest rock-hewn church in Lalibela, and Bete Maryam, a beautiful church with impressive carvings and religious artwork. We also visited Bete Meskel, Bete Denagel, Bete Golgotha, and Bete Mikael. Walking through these churches was an unforgettable experience. The architecture, the underground passages, the stone carvings, and the atmosphere of prayer created a very special feeling. We continued to the second group of churches, which includes Bete Gabriel-Rufael, Bete Merkorios, Bete Amanuel, and Bete Abba Libanos. These churches are connected by courtyards, tunnels, and passages carved into the rock. Each church has its own unique design, history, and religious significance. The family was amazed by the incredible craftsmanship and the spiritual atmosphere of Lalibela.
A Birthday Surprise That Made the Day Even More Special

This day was also very special because it was the adoptive mother’s birthday. Before the trip, I had discussed the birthday surprise with the hotel management and staff. After dinner, we surprised her with a birthday cake. She was so happy, and her husband and children were also delighted. It was a beautiful moment of happiness and celebration. I always love creating special surprises for my clients because after a few days together, they become more than clients. They become family and friends. This birthday celebration was one of those moments I will never forget.
Bete Giyorgis: The Final Wonder of Lalibela

The following morning, after breakfast and checking out of our hotel at around 10:00 AM, we drove to visit the last and most famous rock-hewn church in Lalibela. Bete Giyorgis, also known as St. George’s Church, is one of the most famous and recognizable churches in Ethiopia. It is carved directly into the ground and shaped like a cross when viewed from above. The church is believed to have been built during the reign of King Lalibela and is dedicated to Saint George, the patron saint of Ethiopia. The church is approximately 15 meters deep and is surrounded by a deep trench carved into the rock. Visitors descend into the trench to reach the church, creating a dramatic and unforgettable approach.

Bete Giyorgis is one of the most impressive examples of Ethiopian rock-hewn architecture and is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Lalibela. The family was amazed by the church’s unique design and incredible history. We took pictures, enjoyed the scenery, and spent time appreciating the beauty of this remarkable place. After our visit, we continued our journey back to Addis Ababa.
The Final Family Visit and Our Last Memories in Addis Ababa

After returning to Addis Ababa, we had another special family visit planned. We visited the home of the children’s uncle, where we met his wife and children. We shared lunch, coffee, and a few beautiful hours together, The children enjoyed playing with their cousins, and the atmosphere was full of happiness and love. It was another meaningful opportunity for the family to spend time together before the journey came to an end.

Eventually, it was time to say goodbye once more. Although the reunion had already created so many unforgettable memories, saying goodbye was still difficult. The family had formed a beautiful connection with their Ethiopian relatives, and the siblings had experienced the love and warmth of their biological family. After our final goodbye, we continued our day in Addis Ababa. We went shopping for some of the things that make Ethiopia special. The family wanted to buy teff, the grain used to make injera, Ethiopia’s famous traditional flatbread. Teff is one of Ethiopia’s most important crops and is deeply connected to the country’s food culture. We also bought berbere, the famous Ethiopian spice blend used in many traditional dishes, and frankincense, a traditional aromatic resin used in Ethiopia for religious ceremonies, coffee ceremonies, and cultural traditions. These were meaningful souvenirs to take home and remember their Ethiopian journey.

From there, we visited Beata Mariam Orthodox Church, a place associated with important Ethiopian historical figures. We visited the mausoleum of Emperor Menelik II, Empress Taitu, and Princess Tsehay, the daughter of Emperor Haile Selassie. It was a meaningful opportunity to learn more about Ethiopia’s royal history and the people who shaped the country’s past.

Our next stop was the National Museum of Ethiopia, one of the most important museums in the country. The museum is famous for its archaeological, historical, and cultural collections. One of its most famous treasures is the fossilized remains of Lucy, the ancient hominid discovered in Ethiopia in 1974. The museum also contains ancient artifacts, royal objects, traditional artworks, and exhibitions about Ethiopia’s long history. For visitors, it is an excellent place to understand the depth of Ethiopia’s cultural and historical heritage. After the museum, we drove to Mount Entoto, one of the most beautiful viewpoints overlooking Addis Ababa. Mount Entoto is historically important because it was the location of Emperor Menelik II’s early palace and the place where Addis Ababa developed as Ethiopia’s capital.

The mountain offers panoramic views of the city and the surrounding landscape. We visited the historic area, including the old palace, a small museum, and the church. Unfortunately, it was raining during our visit, but the atmosphere was still beautiful. The misty mountain scenery created a special feeling, and we enjoyed the peaceful surroundings. After a long day of sightseeing, we stopped for ice cream. It was a simple but lovely moment to relax and enjoy a little sweetness before our final evening in Ethiopia. Then we returned to the hotel to pack the family’s bags and prepare for their flight home.
A Final Ethiopian Dinner at Totot Traditional Restaurant

Our final evening in Ethiopia was spent at Totot Traditional Restaurant. We enjoyed a delicious Ethiopian dinner, traditional music, and cultural dancing. It was the perfect way to end an unforgettable journey. The family experienced the flavors, music, and traditions of Ethiopia one more time before returning to Italy. After dinner, we drove to the airport for their midnight flight back to Rome. The journey had come to an end. But the memories would stay with us forever.
A Family Reunion That Will Stay in Our Hearts Forever

This family reunion was truly special. The love between the siblings was amazing. The way they respected each other, cared for each other, and shared every moment together was beautiful to witness. The biological family in Asosa gave us an incredible welcome, with so much food, love, and generosity. The grandparents, uncles, and aunts opened their hearts and their homes to the children and their adoptive family. There were tears, laughter, prayers, family meals, coffee ceremonies, beautiful landscapes, and unforgettable cultural experiences. But most importantly, there was love. Love that crossed distance. Love that crossed borders. Love that brought a family together again.

As a guide, I was deeply honored to be part of this journey. I do not take these moments for granted. Every family reunion is different, and every family has its own story. But the goal is always the same: to help families reconnect, discover their heritage, and create memories that last a lifetime.
How Ethiopian Family Search and Sador Ethiopia Tours Can Help Your Family

At Ethiopian Family Search and Sador Ethiopia Tours, I understand that a heritage reunion trip is much more than a regular holiday. It can be an emotional journey filled with hope, questions, excitement, and sometimes difficult moments. My role is to help make the journey as smooth, comfortable, and meaningful as possible.\ I help families who want to search for their Ethiopian biological relatives and plan a visit to meet them. This includes searching for biological family members, communicating with relatives, helping establish contact, arranging visits to rural areas and family homes, and helping families understand local customs and traditions.

Once the reunion is planned, I can handle the travel arrangements and logistics, including airport pickup and drop-off, domestic flights, transportation, hotel reservations, private drivers, local guides, historical and cultural attractions, restaurant reservations, family meals, translation support, and special surprises.
My goal is to make sure the family can focus on what matters most: spending time together and creating beautiful memories.

I believe that being a guide is not only about showing people places. It is about being there when they need help. It is about understanding their needs, helping with communication, solving unexpected problems, and making sure they feel comfortable and supported throughout their journey. After a few days together, my clients often become friends and family. That is one of the most rewarding parts of my work.
Planning Your Own Ethiopian Heritage Reunion?

If you are planning to visit Ethiopia to meet your biological family, discover your Ethiopian roots, or experience a meaningful heritage journey, I would be happy to help. Whether you are looking for a biological family search, a family reunion trip, a heritage and cultural tour, a visit to your Ethiopian relatives, or a personalized itinerary across Ethiopia, I can help you plan and organize the journey from beginning to end. With Ethiopian Family Search and Sador Ethiopia Tours, you can travel with confidence, knowing that someone is there to support you throughout the journey. Every journey is different. Every family has a story. And every reunion creates memories that last a lifetime. This family’s journey from Asosa to Bahir Dar, Gondar, Lalibela, and Addis Ababa was filled with love, laughter, history, culture, and unforgettable moments. The siblings met their biological family. The family shared meals, prayers, and beautiful experiences. And together, we created memories that will stay in our hearts forever.
As I always say, my goal is simple:
Make Memories and Back to Home with Their Memories.

Thank you to this amazing Italian family for trusting me to be part of such a special journey. It was an honor to walk with you, share these moments, and help make your Ethiopian heritage reunion a beautiful memory.
Until we meet again.

title: Ethiopian New Year
author: Sisay Tilahun
excerpt: There is something special about arriving in Ethiopia in September. After months of rain, the countryside begins to change.

blocks.text: There is something special about arriving in Ethiopia in September. After months of rain, the countryside begins to change. The hills turn green, yellow flowers bloom across the highlands, and the atmosphere becomes full of excitement. Families prepare traditional food, children wear new clothes, and people begin getting ready to welcome a new year.
This is Enkutatash, the Ethiopian New Year.

On September 11, 2026, Ethiopia will welcome the year 2019 according to the Ethiopian calendar. For Ethiopians, this is not simply the beginning of another year. It is a time for family, friendship, faith, culture, and hope. It is a time to remember the past, celebrate the present, and look forward to a new beginning.
If you have ever wanted to understand the heart of Ethiopian culture, Enkutatash is a beautiful place to start.
What Is Enkutatash?

Enkutatash, written in Amharic as እንቁጣጣሽ, is the Ethiopian New Year. It takes place on Meskerem 1, the first day of the Ethiopian calendar. The word Enkutatash is commonly translated as “gift of jewels.” This name is connected to a famous Ethiopian tradition about the Queen of Sheba and her return from Jerusalem. The story has been passed down through generations and remains an important part of the cultural meaning of the holiday. But Enkutatash is about much more than its name. It is a celebration that brings people together. Families visit one another, children sing, traditional food is prepared, and people exchange good wishes for the year ahead. For many Ethiopians living abroad, it is also a special reminder of home. It brings back memories of childhood, family gatherings, traditional food, and the beautiful Ethiopian countryside. When the New Year arrives, people greet each other by saying “Melkam Addis Amet,” which means “Happy New Year.”
Why Does Ethiopia Celebrate New Year in September?

One of the first things visitors notice about Ethiopia is that the country follows its own calendar. While many countries around the world are celebrating 2026, Ethiopia will welcome 2019 on September 11, 2026. The Ethiopian calendar generally falls seven to eight years behind the Gregorian calendar used in most of the world.
This difference comes from historical calendar calculations connected to the date of the birth of Jesus Christ.
The Ethiopian calendar has twelve months of thirty days each, followed by a short thirteenth month called Pagumen. Pagumen contains five days in an ordinary year and six days in a leap year.

The beginning of the Ethiopian year in September is especially beautiful because it comes during a time of seasonal change. The rainy season is coming to an end, the countryside becomes green, and the yellow flowers begin to bloom.
For many Ethiopians, the arrival of the New Year feels like the arrival of a fresh season of life.
It is a time to begin again.
The Beautiful Story of the Queen of Sheba
One of the most interesting stories connected to Enkutatash takes us back to the ancient history of Ethiopia.

According to Ethiopian tradition, the Queen of Sheba was known as Makeda. She was a powerful and wise queen who ruled a kingdom traditionally associated with Ethiopia. The story tells us that she traveled to Jerusalem to meet King Solomon after hearing about his great wisdom and knowledge. Imagine that journey thousands of years ago. The queen traveled with her attendants and brought valuable gifts, including gold, spices, and other treasures. Her visit to King Solomon became one of the most famous stories in Ethiopian tradition. After spending time in Jerusalem, she returned to Ethiopia.

According to the traditional story, the people welcomed her home with gifts of jewels. This is one of the explanations associated with the name Enkutatash, meaning “gift of jewels.” Whether you hear this story from an Ethiopian grandmother, a parent, or a cultural guide, it is a wonderful example of how history and tradition live together in Ethiopia. The story of the Queen of Sheba is not simply about a queen returning from a journey. It is also about welcoming someone home, celebrating an important moment, and sharing happiness with others. That is a beautiful connection to the spirit of the Ethiopian New Year.
The Arrival of Spring and the Yellow Flowers

There is another reason why Enkutatash feels so special. Around the time of the Ethiopian New Year, the countryside begins to come alive with beautiful yellow flowers. These flowers are commonly known as Adey Abeba in Amharic. If you travel through the Ethiopian highlands during this season, you may see fields and hills covered with yellow blossoms. The landscape looks fresh, colorful, and full of life. For many Ethiopians, these flowers are a symbol of the New Year. They remind people that the rainy season is ending and a new season is beginning. They represent hope, beauty, and renewal. Children especially enjoy this time of year. Young girls may gather flowers and visit homes with their friends. They sing traditional New Year songs and share the happiness of the celebration. It is easy to understand why these flowers have become such an important part of Enkutatash. They make the arrival of the New Year visible in the countryside. The land itself seems to be celebrating.
The Joy of Children During Enkutatash

One of the sweetest parts of the Ethiopian New Year is watching children celebrate. In many communities, children wear new clothes and gather together with their friends. Young girls may carry yellow flowers and sing songs as they visit homes in their neighborhoods. Their voices bring a special kind of happiness to the celebration. Parents and neighbors welcome them, and the children enjoy sharing the excitement of the New Year. For many Ethiopian children, Enkutatash is a day full of wonderful memories. It is a time for new clothes, family visits, traditional food, singing, and spending time with friends. As people grow older, these childhood memories often remain close to their hearts. Years later, someone living far away from Ethiopia may still remember the sound of children singing on New Year’s Day, the smell of coffee being prepared at home, and the joy of visiting relatives. These are the small moments that make a celebration meaningful.
Preparing the Home for the New Year

Before Enkutatash arrives, many Ethiopian families begin preparing their homes. The house may be cleaned, traditional food is prepared, and families get ready to welcome relatives and friends. In some homes, parents buy new clothes for their children. In others, family members travel from different towns and cities to spend the holiday together. The preparation itself becomes part of the celebration. There is a special feeling when a family is getting ready for an important holiday. The kitchen becomes busy, relatives begin arriving, and everyone looks forward to spending time together. In Ethiopia, hospitality is an important part of family life, and Enkutatash is a wonderful opportunity to share that hospitality with others. A guest who visits an Ethiopian home during the New Year may be welcomed with coffee, food, conversation, and warm wishes.
Traditional Ethiopian Food During Enkutatash

Food is one of the most important parts of Ethiopian celebrations. During Enkutatash, families prepare traditional dishes and gather around the table to enjoy a special meal together. Injera is often at the center of the meal. This traditional Ethiopian flatbread is served with different kinds of stews, vegetables, and meat dishes. Doro wat, a spicy chicken stew made with berbere, onions, and other spices, is a popular dish for major celebrations. Other families may prepare tibs, vegetables, lentils, or their own favorite traditional foods. The food may be different from one family to another, but the meaning is often the same. People are sharing. People are welcoming one another. People are enjoying the company of family and friends. A New Year meal is not just about what is on the plate. It is about the conversations around the table, the laughter, the stories, and the feeling of being together. For visitors to Ethiopia, experiencing a traditional Ethiopian meal during Enkutatash can be a wonderful cultural memory.
The Ethiopian Coffee Ceremony: A Moment of Togetherness

No story about Ethiopian culture would feel complete without mentioning coffee. Ethiopia is famous for its coffee traditions, and the traditional coffee ceremony is an important part of social life. During the New Year, families and friends may gather for a coffee ceremony at home. The ceremony usually begins with roasting green coffee beans. The rich smell of the freshly roasted coffee fills the room. The beans are then ground and brewed in a traditional clay pot called a jebena. The coffee is served in small cups, often with snacks such as popcorn or roasted grains. But the ceremony is about much more than coffee. It is a time to sit together, talk, laugh, and enjoy the company of others. During Enkutatash, the coffee ceremony creates a warm and welcoming atmosphere. Relatives who have not seen each other for a long time can sit together and share stories. A visitor may arrive as a stranger and leave feeling like part of the family. That is one of the beautiful things about Ethiopian hospitality.
Traditional Clothing and the Beauty of the Celebration

Enkutatash is also a time when many Ethiopians wear new or special clothes. For women and girls, the traditional Habesha kemis is a beautiful part of the celebration. The white cotton dress, often decorated with colorful woven borders known as tibeb, reflects the elegance of Ethiopian traditional clothing. Men and boys may also wear traditional white clothing or modern outfits for the holiday. The streets can become colorful with people dressed for church, family visits, and celebrations. For visitors, seeing Ethiopian families wearing traditional clothing during the New Year is a wonderful way to experience the country’s cultural beauty. The clothing, flowers, music, food, and family gatherings all come together to create the atmosphere of Enkutatash.
Enkutatash and the Importance of Family

For many Ethiopians, the New Year is deeply connected to family. It is a time when relatives come together, even if they live far apart. Children visit their parents and grandparents. Brothers and sisters meet. Friends and neighbors exchange greetings. Some people travel long distances to spend the holiday with their loved ones. Others may not be able to travel, but they still call family members or send messages to wish them a happy new year. For Ethiopians living abroad, Enkutatash can be an especially emotional time. It may remind them of their childhood, their hometown, their parents, and the traditions they grew up with. A simple New Year greeting can bring back many memories. It can remind someone of the smell of coffee at home, the taste of their mother’s cooking, or the sound of family members laughing together. This is why Enkutatash is so much more than a date on the calendar. It is a celebration of belonging.
A New Year Story: Returning Home to Ethiopia

Imagine an Ethiopian who has been living abroad for many years. Life has taken them far away from home. They have built a new life in another country, but they still remember celebrating Enkutatash as a child. They remember the yellow flowers. They remember the traditional food. They remember visiting relatives and hearing the New Year greetings. One year, they decide to return to Ethiopia for the New Year. As the plane arrives in Addis Ababa, they feel a familiar excitement. The sounds of the city, the people, and the atmosphere begin to bring back old memories.They travel to their hometown and arrive at the family home. Their mother is waiting. Their father is smiling. Relatives begin arriving, and the house becomes full of conversation and laughter. Coffee is prepared. Food is served. Stories are shared. The family sits together and talks about the years that have passed. For this person, the New Year becomes more than a celebration. It becomes a moment of reconnecting with family and remembering where they come from. The yellow flowers outside the house remind them of childhood. The coffee reminds them of home. The family gathering reminds them that some connections remain strong, no matter how many years have passed. This is the spirit of Enkutatash.
Enkutatash in Addis Ababa

Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia, is a wonderful place to experience the New Year. During the holiday season, the city becomes lively with families, visitors, cultural activities, and preparations for the celebration. People travel from different parts of the country to visit relatives and spend time together. The city also offers many opportunities to discover Ethiopian history and culture.\ Visitors can explore traditional markets, enjoy Ethiopian food, experience a coffee ceremony, and discover the city’s historic and cultural attractions. The surrounding highlands offer beautiful scenery, especially during the seasonal transition around September. A visit to Entoto, the mountain overlooking Addis Ababa, can provide wonderful views of the city and a chance to experience the beauty of the Ethiopian highlands. For travelers who want to understand Ethiopia beyond its famous landmarks, spending time in Addis Ababa during Enkutatash can be a memorable cultural experience.
Enkutatash and Ethiopia’s Diverse Cultural Heritage

Ethiopia is home to many different cultural communities, languages, traditions, and ways of life. Although Enkutatash is the widely recognized Ethiopian New Year, different communities across the country also have their own traditional celebrations. One example is Gifaataa, a traditional New Year festival associated with the Wolayta people in southern Ethiopia. Gifaataa has its own cultural traditions, songs, food, and community celebrations. This is a reminder that Ethiopia’s heritage is wonderfully diverse. The New Year may feel different in Addis Ababa, Gondar, Bahir Dar, Hosaena, Arba Minch, or other parts of the country. Each community has its own customs. Each family has its own way of celebrating. And every tradition adds something beautiful to the cultural story of Ethiopia. For visitors, this diversity is one of the most rewarding things about exploring the country.
The Spiritual Meaning of the Ethiopian New Year

For many Ethiopians, Enkutatash is also a time of spiritual reflection. The Ethiopian Orthodox Christian tradition gives great importance to prayer, church services, and religious observances. During the New Year, many people attend church, give thanks, and pray for blessings for the year ahead. They may pray for peace, family unity, good health, prosperity, and happiness. For some people, Enkutatash is mainly a religious celebration. For others, it is a cultural holiday. For many, it is both. The important thing is that the New Year creates a moment to reflect on life and look forward with hope. It is a chance to think about the past year and the future. It is a chance to forgive, reconnect, and begin again.
Why Enkutatash Is Special for Ethiopians Abroad

For Ethiopians living outside the country, the New Year can be a very meaningful occasion. Even when they are far away from their homeland, many people continue to celebrate Enkutatash with family and friends. Some prepare traditional Ethiopian food. Some attend cultural gatherings. Some call their relatives in Ethiopia. Some teach their children about the Ethiopian calendar and traditional New Year customs. For the younger generation growing up abroad, Enkutatash can be a way to learn about their Ethiopian heritage. It helps them understand the traditions of their parents and grandparents. It gives them a connection to the country, the culture, and the family stories that came before them. In this way, the New Year continues to connect generations.
Why Visitors Should Experience Enkutatash in Ethiopia

If you are planning to visit Ethiopia, experiencing Enkutatash can be a wonderful opportunity to see the country from a different perspective. You can discover the beauty of the Ethiopian highlands during the flower season. You can learn about the Ethiopian calendar and the ancient traditions connected to it. You can enjoy traditional Ethiopian food and coffee. You can see families wearing traditional clothing and celebrating together. You can hear New Year songs and experience the warmth of Ethiopian hospitality. Most importantly, you can experience a celebration that is deeply connected to the people and culture of Ethiopia. Traveling during Enkutatash is not just about visiting a destination. It is about being part of a special moment in the life of the country.
A New Year Message from Ethiopia

As Ethiopia welcomes the year 2019, the country celebrates another beginning. The yellow flowers bloom across the highlands. Families gather around traditional meals. Coffee is prepared and shared. Children sing and celebrate. Friends exchange greetings. People remember the past and look forward to the future. Enkutatash reminds us that life is full of new beginnings. It reminds us of the importance of family, friendship, and cultural heritage. It reminds us that even after difficult times, there is always room for hope. And it reminds us that some of the most beautiful moments in life are the simple ones we share with the people we love. Whether you are in Ethiopia, living abroad, or planning your first visit to the country, the spirit of Enkutatash is a beautiful invitation to celebrate life and new beginnings.
Melkam Addis Amet 2019!
Happy Ethiopian New Year 2019! May this new year bring peace, happiness, good health, prosperity, and beautiful new beginnings to all Ethiopian families and friends around the world.

title: When Roots Come Home
author: Sisay Tilahun
excerpt: A Journey of Reconnection, Renewal, and Greatness in Southern Ethiopia, Return Part Nothing is more delightful than arriving at Bole International Airport! Last year, June 18th, I am honored to host four extraordinary adopting…

blocks.text: A Journey of Reconnection, Renewal, and Greatness in Southern Ethiopia, Return Part
Arrival in Addis Ababa

Nothing is more delightful than arriving at Bole International Airport! Last year, June 18th, I am honored to host four extraordinary adopting families and their children for the first time. Most of the families in Addis Ababa had been connected to my biological family search work at Ethiopian Family Search long ago. It felt incredibly special to re-connect them and give a tour of the country through the exceptional service of Sador Ethiopia Tours.

After arriving at the hotel, we started exploring the place and went to the National Museum to see Lucy on the first afternoon. We enjoyed a scrumptious traditional lunch and then hiked up lovely eucalyptus trees on Mount Entoto. Enjoying magnificent views of Addis Ababa, visiting the old palace, and having fun in the mountainous cool air made a wonderful introduction.
Reconnection, Culture, and Coffee

Having arrived from another continent, I believe it is essential to take it easy and let people relax and get used to the surroundings. We spent a lovely morning at Holy Trinity Cathedral, enjoying the amazing arts. Our afternoon was well spent at Mercato – one of the most excellent open-air markets in Africa, taking in the astonishing colors, exotic spices, and unique handcrafted souvenirs.
First Family Reunion

We loaded our coaster bus to drive back to Hosaena, which is about 230 km from Addis Ababa, and I think it was the best thing that could have happened. Just a few kilometers from Hosaena, we took a short break in another village near our first destination to witness a spectacular family reunion. An adopted boy was about to see his birth family for the first time after returning to Ethiopia. The local family has made a remarkable traditional ceremony to welcome him back. Over a delicious lunch, coffee, and stories, the language barrier melted away. Heartfelt crying, warm hugs, and laughter filled the house as no one could believe this moment had come. This was one of those priceless, once-in-a-lifetime experiences that you want to frame and hang on your heart. We took numerous photos!
School Project Opening and Family Reunion

The next day, we drove to Amecho Primary School in Doyo Gena to officially open a new latrine facility. Strides for Africa and Roots Ethiopia construct this excellent project, and we arrived at the school to be greeted with flower bouquets, traditional shawls, and beaming faces by the students, teachers, and local elders.

We offered traditional bread, drank coffee and shared stories with them. Gifts of sports balls and playful flags for the children brightened their day! The founder of Strides for Africa and my adopting dad also gave an inspiring speech to the community.

In the afternoon, we drove to a small village called Utuge. The founder’s adopted son reunites with his birth mother, grandfather, great-grandmother, aunts, and uncles for the first time since 2009. I will be forever grateful for this beautiful reunion. The family members sit together, drink coffee, tell stories, and feel the warmth of being together after a long and heartfelt journey.
Mount Hambericho: Steps and Miracles

We went sightseeing on an adventure to Mount Hambericho in Durame. After leaving the tarred road, we entered a forest of rocks and mountains. The coaster bus had difficulty going up a steep slope and lost power! We quickly hired local drivers familiar with rocky paths to take us up and had a great time! This was one of those heartwarming local adventures.

Hiking Mount Hambericho has been described as an easy walk up a long staircase. Well, I walked up a staircase of 777 steps and reached the summit! The view was fantastic as I enjoyed a 360-degree view of the beautiful southern green hills. On the way back to Hosaena from Mount Hambericho, you might ask, what else could possibly happen? As we dropped off the family in Doyo Gena town, I received a call from my local liaison. He asked me if I could arrange to meet the birth mother at the Doyo Gena district office in the morning. She has recently remarried and moved from the northern part of Ethiopia. What a pleasant surprise to have such a delightful family connection happen in town!
Farewell in Addis Ababa

Before going back to Addis Ababa, we stopped by the first family again to spend more time together. In the meantime, another family reunited with the local researcher who helped them trace their daughter’s roots for a more extended period. We all met in Addis Ababa in the evening for a farewell dinner.

Sador Ethiopia Tour hosted a traditional farewell dinner at an elegant Ethiopian traditional restaurant. Kids and their parents danced the night away to traditional music and delicious meals in a spectacular party. What a tremendous end it was to an amazing family reunion tour!

title: Entoto Natural Park
author: Sisay Tilahun
excerpt: A Guide to Entoto Natural Park: Nature, History, and Panoramic Views Above Addis Ababa Rising over 3,000 meters (9,800 feet) above sea level, Mount Entoto is the green heart of Addis Ababa. Covered in dense eucalyptus forests,…

blocks.text: A Guide to Entoto Natural Park: Nature, History, and Panoramic Views Above Addis Ababa

Rising over 3,000 meters (9,800 feet) above sea level, Mount Entoto is the green heart of Addis Ababa. Covered in dense eucalyptus forests, Entoto offers fresh mountain air, breathtaking views of the capital below, and a deep connection to Ethiopia’s royal history.

Once the 19th-century royal seat of Emperor Menelik II, Entoto has recently been transformed into Entoto Natural Park—a world-class eco-tourism destination featuring walking trails, adventure sports, and peaceful nature spots.
1. Visit the Royal Palace of Emperor Menelik II

Before Addis Ababa became the capital in 1886, Emperor Menelik II and Empress Taitu ruled from the top of Mount Entoto. Today, you can step inside the historic wooden palace and visit the nearby Entoto Maryam Church, where Menelik II was crowned emperor. The small on-site museum displays royal robes, crowns, and historical artifacts.
2. Enjoy Adventure & Outdoor Activities
Entoto Natural Park is ideal for outdoor enthusiasts of all ages:
Ziplining: Glide through the eucalyptus canopy on one of the longest ziplines in East Africa.
Mountain Biking & Hiking: Follow miles of paved and forest trails designed for smooth walking, running, or cycling.
Rope Courses & Paintball: Fun outdoor activities for families and group travelers.
3. Relax in Nature & Enjoy Local Cuisine

After exploring the trails, relax at one of the park’s eco-friendly cafes or restaurants. Enjoy a traditional Ethiopian coffee ceremony surrounded by fresh mountain breezes, or sample local dishes while taking in sweeping views of Addis Ababa below.
Practical Information for Visitors
Location: Northern edge of Addis Ababa (approx. 30–40 minutes drive from the city center).
Opening Hours: Open daily from early morning until evening.
Best Time to Visit: Morning or late afternoon for clear views and mild temperatures.
What to Bring: A light jacket or sweater (it gets cool at high altitude), comfortable walking shoes, and a camera.
Travel Tip: Combining a morning visit to the National Museum with an afternoon trip to Entoto Park makes for a perfect 1-day Addis Ababa itinerary!

title: The National Museum of Ethiopia
author: Sisay Tilahun
excerpt: The Complete Guide to the National Museum of Ethiopia: 3.2 Million Years of History in Addis Ababa When your journey in Ethiopia begins in Addis Ababa, there is one place you simply cannot miss: the National Museum of Ethiopia.…

blocks.text: The Complete Guide to the National Museum of Ethiopia: 3.2 Million Years of History in Addis Ababa

When your journey in Ethiopia begins in Addis Ababa, there is one place you simply cannot miss: the National Museum of Ethiopia. Situated between Arat Kilo and Sidist Kilo, this world-renowned museum holds the keys to human origins, royal dynasties, sacred art, and rich cultural traditions.
Whether you are a history lover, a photography enthusiast, or a family exploring Africa for the first time, this complete guide will help you discover everything the museum has to offer.
A Brief Story of the Museum
The story of the National Museum is as fascinating as the treasures inside it:
1944: The museum began as a small public exhibition inside the National Library, featuring ceremonial costumes donated by the Ethiopian Royal Family.
1952–1955: The Institute of Archaeology was founded, leading to major archaeological discoveries in northern Ethiopia.
1966–1967: The museum moved to its historic Old Building—a structure originally built in 1935 that later served as a royal residence for Prince Mekonnen and then as the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
1978–1981: With support from USAID and UNESCO consultants, the New Building was designed and built to serve as the main exhibition hall.

2001 to Present: The permanent collection was fully reorganized in the main hall to feature incredible ancient hominid fossils and archaeological discoveries from Hadar, Middle Awash, and the Omo Valley.
Exploring the 4 Main Exhibition Galleries
The main museum building is organized into four distinct sections across its floors:
1. Paleoanthropological & Pre-Historic Section (The Basement)
This is the heart of human origins. Here, you will stand face-to-face with world-famous hominid fossils and stone tools dating back millions of years:
Lucy (Dinkinesh): The celebrated 3.2-million-year-old Australopithecus afarensis skeleton discovered in Hadar in 1974.
Selam: The remarkably preserved fossil of a 3.3-million-year-old child (often called “Lucy’s baby”).
Ardi: A hominid fossil dating back an astonishing 4.4 million years.
2. Pre-Axumite to 20th Century Historical Section (Ground Floor)

Travel back in time through Ethiopia’s ancient civilizations and royal empires. You will see pre-Axumite stone carvings, ancient pottery, minted Aksumite coins, royal crowns, ceremonial thrones, and historical scripts that demonstrate a sophisticated way of life spanning thousands of years.
3. The Art Section (First Floor)
Featuring over 1,500 traditional and modern artworks, this gallery shows the evolution of Ethiopian visual culture:
Traditional Christian Art: Unsigned religious icons and church paintings created by priest-artists over hundreds of years.

Contemporary Masterpieces: Works by legendary Ethiopian artists from 1950 to 2005, including Maitre Artist World Laureate Afework Tekle (the museum houses over 80 of his works) and Gebre Kristos Desta.
4. The Ethnographic Section (Second Floor)

Ethiopia is home to more than 80 distinct ethnic groups. This vibrant section showcases traditional clothing, musical instruments, household items, weapons, and tools, celebrating the diversity and shared heritage of the Ethiopian people.
Useful Information for Your Visit
Location: Amest Kilo (between Arat Kilo and Sidist Kilo), King George VI Street, Addis Ababa.
Opening Hours: Open daily except Monday from 8:30 AM to 5:00 PM.
Best Time to Spend: Plan for 1.5 to 2.5 hours to enjoy all four galleries comfortably.
Pro Tip: Exploring the museum with a knowledgeable local guide brings these ancient artifacts to life with stories you won’t find on the display cards!

title: Ashenda
author: Sisay Tilahun
excerpt: Ashenda/Ashendye is a unique Northern Ethiopia traditional festival which takes place in August to mark the ending of fasting called Filseta. This event is mostly for girls and young women, which they await very eagerly every…

blocks.text: Ashenda/Ashendye is a unique Northern Ethiopia traditional festival which takes place in August to mark the ending of fasting called Filseta. This event is mostly for girls and young women, which they await very eagerly every year. The name of the festival “Ashenda” comes from the name of a tall grass that the girls make in to a skirt and ware it around their waist as a decoration. The young women and girls dress the best traditional dresses called Tilfie which is a cotton dress decorated with amazing embroidery from the neck to toe in front of the dress. The girls also adorned themselves with array of beautiful jewelry. After they gather in the village or city center they divide in to small groups and they go house to house singing and playing their drums. They stop at ever house and sing and dance for the people in the houses. It is customary for people to give them money, food and drinks and other items for their efforts. Be a part of this vibrating and intriguing festival in all parts of Tigray and the northern part of the Amhara region.

title: Hoya Hoye! Unveiling the Tradition of Buhe
author: Sisay Tilahun
excerpt: In the heart of Ethiopia’s rainy season, as the landscape turns a vibrant green, a special celebration unfolds. This is Buhe, a unique and joyful holiday observed by the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church on August 19th.

blocks.text: In the heart of Ethiopia’s rainy season, as the landscape turns a vibrant green, a special celebration unfolds. This is Buhe, a unique and joyful holiday observed by the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church on August 19th. Unlike many holidays celebrated with grand church ceremonies, Buhe is a celebration of community, and it’s a day when the voices of young boys echo through the neighborhoods, carrying a message of good wishes and blessings.

The holiday commemorates the Transfiguration of Jesus on Mount Tabor, a pivotal moment in Christian theology. While the religious significance is profound, the popular tradition of Buhe is carried out by young boys who participate in a ritual known as “Hoya Hoye.” Groups of boys, often dressed in traditional attire, gather and go from door to door, singing a special song. The lyrics are a heartfelt expression of praise for the homeowners, wishing them prosperity and a bountiful year ahead. It’s a charming exchange that strengthens community bonds and passes on a cherished tradition to the next generation.

Central to the “Hoya Hoye” tradition are the rhythmic instruments used by the boys. Eschewing drums and other common musical instruments, the boys carry simple sticks and a unique homemade instrument—a collection of bottle caps that, when shaken, create a lively jingle. As they sing, they hit the ground with their sticks, adding a percussive beat to their melodies. Another notable sound is the loud crack of a whip, known as a jiraaf. This sound is said to symbolize the thunder that accompanied the voice of God during the Transfiguration, adding a powerful and symbolic element to the festivities.

In return for their songs and good wishes, the homeowners offer the boys a reward. Traditionally, they receive freshly baked bread called mulmul, a delicious treat made specifically for the occasion. In modern times, it is also common for the boys to be given money. As night falls, the final act of the Buhe celebration takes place with the lighting of a bonfire, known as a chibo. The glowing flames symbolize the radiant light of the Transfiguration, bringing a beautiful and spiritual conclusion to a day filled with song, tradition, and community spirit.
